title: Stopping or continuing RAS-inhibitor medicines before surgery
official: Stopping or continuing RAS-inhibitor drugs before major elective non-cardiac surgery
summary:
Background and study aims
Many people take medicines called renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, such as ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), to treat high blood pressure, heart failure or kidney disease. When people taking these medicines need major surgery, doctors must decide whether the medicines should be continued or temporarily stopped around the time of the operation. Both approaches may affect blood pressure during and after surgery and could influence the risk of complications. Currently, there is uncertainty about which approach is best. This study aims to determine whether stopping or continuing RAS inhibitor medicines before major elective non-cardiac surgery leads to better recovery and health outcomes.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 50 years and older who are awaiting major elective non-cardiac surgery and are currently taking a RAS inhibitor medicine (an ACE inhibitor and/or ARB).

What does the study involve?
Participants are randomly allocated to one of two groups between five and ten days before surgery. Those in the stop group stop taking their RAS inhibitor medicine for three days before surgery and restart it four days after surgery. Those in the continue group continue taking their medication as usual before and after surgery. Information on blood pressure, laboratory results and cardiovascular medications is collected during the seven-day intervention period. Participants are followed up 30 days and 180 days after surgery to assess their recovery, health outcomes and quality of life.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The study may help identify the safest and most effective way to manage RAS inhibitor medicines around the time of surgery, improving care for future patients. Participants may not receive a direct benefit from taking part. 

The medicinal products involved in the trial (RAS-inhibitor drugs) are licensed in the UK and will be used within their licensed range of indications, dosage and form. Patients will already be on the medication prior to enrolment. The main risks of stopping RAS inhibitor medicine are strokes and damage to the heart. The main risks of continuing are damage to the heart and kidneys. Only a small number of people experience these problems, and they are the same whether they join the trial or not. Joining the study will therefore have very few risks beyond those of normal care.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by Queen Mary University of London, UK, and is currently recruiting participants through NHS hospitals in the UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to March 2030.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Principal Investigator: Dr Tom Abbott, t.abbott@qmul.ac.uk
conditions: Adult patients undergoing major elective non-cardiac surgery
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients aged ≥50 years, awaiting major elective non-cardiac surgery, and taking a RAS-inhibitor (ACE-i and/or ARB with a single active ingredient formulation)
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Inability or refusal to provide informed consent
2.	Clinician refusal to allow a patient to participate
